catalog_quote: During a year of fieldwork (1979-80) the tonal systems of each of these dialects were studied, and it is on the basis of this comparative information that the reconstruction of the tonal system of the protolanguage is attempted. [...] 2. RIFT VALLEY GROUP (KIPSIKIIS-MARKWETA) 2.1 TONAL PROCESSES These languages have either three (H,L,F) or four (H,L,F,F̲) surface tones. The three-tone languages are Kipsikiis and Markweta. Nandi, Tuken, and Keyo have four tones. All languages have three underlying tonemes (H,L,F). [...] Low Raising In Nandi, Keyo and Tuken low tones are raised to mid-level after high tones. [...] High Fall Lowering (HFL) In Nandi, Keyo and Tuken underlying high falling tones are converted to low falling tones following a low tone or word initially. [...] Final Fall (FF) In Nandi and Keyo virtually all final high tones are converted to falling tones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Keyo (Keiyo) is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language: three underlying tonemes (High, Low, Falling) with four surface tones (H, L, high-fall, low-fall), plus dialect-specific tone rules; no statement about word stress or a stress accent is made in this or any other opened Keiyo source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal detail: Rising Tone realisation of long-vowel H after pause/L is 'less frequently heard in Keyo'; Final Fall applies fully only in Nandi and Keyo.
new_statements.domain_note: Nominal word-level tonology (primary/secondary noun forms, citation forms). The same tonal-only picture is given first-hand for Keiyo proper by native-speaker authors Kiprop & Chepkirui 2014 (IJHSS 4(6(1)) p. 143: roots M/ML, suffixed plurals L..H) and Kiprop, Chepkirui & Kibet 2015 (RHSS 5(15) p. 14: 'three underlying tones.. High (H), Low (L) and Mid (M)'), neither of which states a stress rule. The only known explicit treatment of stress ('Druckakzent') for Kalenjin incl. Keyo is Rottland 1982 sec. 5.1.3.2 (pp. 77-78), not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Creider 1981 writes 'Keyo' (= Keiyo/Elgeyo, keiy1238) as one of the Rift Valley Kalenjin dialects studied in his 1979-80 fieldwork; the statement is dialect-specific within a comparative paper. Kiprop et al. 2014/2015 describe Keiyo of Tambach Division (Keiyo North), same glottocode. Local & Lodge's 'Kalenjin' data are Tugen (tuge1241), not Keiyo, and were excluded.

sources.note: First-hand (fieldwork 1979-80 on each Kalenjin dialect incl. Keyo): Keyo has four surface tones, three underlying tonemes (H, L, F); Keyo-specific tone rules listed (Low Raising, Rising Tone, High Fall Lowering, Final Fall shared with Nandi). Nothing said about word stress or accent.
